title: Graft back
hookLine: a branch cut from its neighbor is cut from the whole tree, but we can be grafted back (Meditations 11.8)
carry: a clean cut, not a ragged one

cards: Scroll far enough down a contact list and there may be a name that's gone quiet for years. Nobody fought.

Maybe there was one small sting, a missed wedding, a comment that landed wrong, and then it was easier not to reply. Then easier again. Now the gap feels too big to cross, and every month it gets a little bigger.
Gardeners know something about this. You can cut a branch off an apple tree and, with a clean cut and a little binding, fit it back onto living wood, and it grows. That's called grafting.
Marcus Aurelius borrows the gardeners' picture.

teach.h: CUT FROM ONE, CUT FROM THE WHOLE.
teach.b: Book Eleven of the Meditations. Marcus is looking at a tree. In George Long's 1862 translation: "A branch cut off from the adjacent branch must of necessity be cut off from the whole tree also."
For Marcus, a person belongs to a great shared community, the whole human city, and falling out with one person is falling a little way out of all of it. Then comes the twist.

A branch doesn't cut itself off; someone else takes the saw to it. A person, Marcus says, does it alone, by hating someone and turning away, and doesn't even notice he's cut himself off from the whole.
But Marcus says we have a gift the branch doesn't: we can grow back to the one near us, and become part of the whole again. Graft back. Then, being Marcus, he adds a caution.

If the cutting happens again and again, the joining gets harder. The gardeners say a branch that grew with the tree isn't quite the same as one grafted back after being cut. So don't make a habit of the saw.
Think about what a real graft needs.
A clean cut, not a ragged one.
Two living surfaces pressed close. Something to bind them. And time, while the wood knits.
That's not a bad description of reconnecting with a person: a simple, honest message, actually showing up, patience while it heals.

how: Readers of Marcus Aurelius often take Meditations 11.8 as a prompt to repair a drifted relationship: one short, honest message rather than waiting for the perfect moment.

to rejoin the whole after cutting yourself off
to cut away a dead branch so the tree thrives

games.q: you've drifted from a friend for two years. no fight, just silence. what does Marcus's tree suggest?
o: wait for them to go first.
let it go; the branch is gone.
games.why: Marcus says a person has a gift the branch lacks: we can grow back to our neighbor. he also warns not to make the cutting a habit.

practice: Let one name come, someone you've drifted from without a real reason; not someone who hurt you badly, since some cuts are right to keep, just a drift.
Picture their face, notice what's in the gap, pride, awkwardness, simple time, and then picture the first plain sentence you could send: thought of you today, how are you? Hold it gently.

wordCard.voice: Graft back. Marcus's picture of a branch rejoining the tree: cut from one person, you're cut from the whole, and you can grow back. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: a clean cut, not a ragged one. No long apology needed, just the reaching. Until tomorrow.
